newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli December CPI seen rising 0.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Israeli December CPI seen rising 0.7 pct.

text.p: Israel's December consumer price index (CPI), due to be published on Wednesday, will show a rise of about 0.7 percent, economists predicted on Tuesday.
An 0.7 percent rise in the CPI for the month would bring the full-year 1996 inflation rate to about 10.5 percent.
"If there is a surprise (for December), I expect it will be towards lower inflation," said Hezy Gutman, head of the economics department at First International Bank of Israel.

December will mark a continuation in the sharp drop in inflation that began in July 1996. Gutman attributed the decline to slower growth, if not declines, in housing prices and a drop in underlying inflation.
"Inflation has entered the (government's) target zone of seven to 10 percent, and it is certainly under control," said Ptachia Bar Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim.

Hapoalim is forecasting 8.5 inflation for all of 1997, with housing prices serving as a key moderating factor. "We believe that housing prices will rise less than the index, about half or four percent," he said.

The Bank of Israel's continued policy of monetary restraint will also cool inflation as will the slowing economy. The Treasury expects gross domestic product to expand about four percent this year, down from an estimated 4.4 percent in 1996.
Gutman said the only thing he saw that could accelerate consumer prices was a large depreciation of the shekel, an event he deemed unlikely.

Bar Shavit said it was unclear whether the central bank would lower interest rates in February. He said at most the bank would cut the base rate by 0.5 percentage from the current 14.7 percent. Gutman said he he expected an 0.2-0.3 point cut, assuming December inflation was 0.7 percent.
The Bank of Israel is due to announce its February monetary programme on January 27.
Although the slowing economy should influence the bank to cut the base rate, the central bank will likely take into account the increased liquidity in the economy, Bar Shavit said.
Newspaper reports said on Tuesday that the Bank of Israel planned to increase liquidity requirements on bank deposits by about five percentage points. If so, that would lower deposit rates.
The bank would not comment on the report.

At the same time, the big rise in the government's December budget deficit pumped liquidity in the economy, which unconfirmed newspaper reports today said increased money supply by three percent in the month.
